'''Maslov index''' is an [[integer-valued]] invariant in [[symplectic geometry]], [[microlocal analysis]], and [[semiclassical physics|semiclassical analysis]]. It is associated most classically with a loop or path of [[Lagrangian subspace]]s in a symplectic vector space, and measures how that path meets a distinguished singular hypersurface known as the ''Maslov cycle''.<ref name="Arnold1967">{{cite journal
 |last=Arnold
 |first=V. I.
 |author-link=Vladimir Arnold
 |title=On a characteristic class entering in conditions of quantization
 |journal=Functional Analysis and Its Applications
 |volume=1
 |issue=1
 |year=1967
 |pages=1–13
}}</ref><ref name="RobbinSalamon1993">{{cite journal
 |last1=Robbin
 |first1=Joel
 |last2=Salamon
 |first2=Dietmar
 |title=The Maslov index for paths
 |journal=Topology
 |volume=32
 |issue=4
 |year=1993
 |pages=827–844
 |doi=10.1016/0040-9383(93)90052-W
}}</ref> Informally, it records the winding of a family of Lagrangian subspaces relative to the locus of subspaces that fail to be transverse to a chosen reference Lagrangian.<ref name="McDuffSalamon2017">{{cite book
 |last1=McDuff
 |first1=Dusa
 |last2=Salamon
 |first2=Dietmar
 |title=Introduction to Symplectic Topology
 |edition=3rd
 |publisher=Oxford University Press
 |year=2017
 |isbn=978-0-19-879489-9
}}</ref>

The Maslov index was introduced in the context of asymptotic methods in mathematical physics and later reformulated in topological and geometric terms.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="LionVergne1980">{{cite book
 |last1=Lion
 |first1=Gérard
 |last2=Vergne
 |first2=Michèle
 |title=The Weil Representation, Maslov Index and Theta Series
 |series=Progress in Mathematics
 |publisher=Birkhäuser
 |location=Boston
 |year=1980
 |isbn=978-0-8176-3007-2
 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4684-9154-8
}}</ref> It plays an important role in the theory of [[Fourier integral operator]]s, [[geometric quantization]], [[Hamiltonian system]]s, [[spectral theory]], and [[Floer homology]].<ref name="Hormander1971">{{cite journal
 |last=Hörmander
 |first=Lars |author-link=Lars Hörmander
 |title=Fourier integral operators. I
 |journal=Acta Mathematica
 |volume=127
 |year=1971
 |pages=79–183
 |doi=10.1007/BF02392052
}}</ref><ref name="Duistermaat1996">{{cite book
 |last=Duistermaat
 |first=J. J.
 |title=Fourier Integral Operators
 |series=Progress in Mathematics
 |volume=130
 |publisher=Birkhäuser
 |location=Boston
 |year=1996
 |isbn=978-0-8176-8107-4
}}</ref><ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" />

== Overview ==

Let <math>(V,\omega)</math> be a finite-dimensional symplectic vector space, and let <math>\Lambda(V)</math> denote its [[Lagrangian Grassmannian]], the manifold of all Lagrangian subspaces of <math>V</math>. The topology of <math>\Lambda(V)</math> is nontrivial: its [[fundamental group]] is isomorphic to <math>\mathbf{Z}</math>. The Maslov index may be viewed as the corresponding [[homotopy invariant]], assigning an integer to a loop in the Lagrangian Grassmannian.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" />

Equivalently, after fixing a reference Lagrangian subspace <math>L_0</math>, one considers the ''Maslov cycle''
:<math>\Sigma(L_0)=\{L\in \Lambda(V)\mid L\cap L_0\neq 0\}.</math>
This is a singular hypersurface in <math>\Lambda(V)</math>. For a generic path of Lagrangian subspaces, the Maslov index counts with signs the intersections of the path with <math>\Sigma(L_0)</math>.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

== Definition ==

=== As a homotopy invariant ===

If <math>\gamma\colon S^1\to \Lambda(V)</math> is a loop in the Lagrangian Grassmannian, its Maslov index <math>\mu(\gamma)</math> is the integer corresponding to the [[homotopy class]] of <math>\gamma</math> under the isomorphism
:<math>\pi_1(\Lambda(V))\cong \mathbf{Z}.</math><ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" />

This definition makes the Maslov index a topological invariant of loops of Lagrangian subspaces.<ref name="Arnold1967" />

=== Via the Maslov cycle ===

Fix a Lagrangian subspace <math>L_0\subseteq V</math>. For a sufficiently generic path <math>\gamma\colon [a,b]\to \Lambda(V)</math> whose endpoints are transverse to <math>L_0</math>, the Maslov index <math>\mu_{L_0}(\gamma)</math> is defined as the signed intersection number of <math>\gamma</math> with the Maslov cycle <math>\Sigma(L_0)</math>.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

At a transverse crossing time <math>t_*</math> for which <math>\gamma(t_*)\cap L_0\neq 0</math>, the sign is determined by the ''crossing form'', a [[quadratic form]] on the intersection <math>\gamma(t_*)\cap L_0</math>. The total Maslov index is the sum of the [[inertial index]] of these crossing forms over all crossings.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

=== Via the Kashiwara form ===

Given a cycle of Lagrangian subspaces <math>A_1\to A_2\dots\to A_k\to A_1</math>, the '''Kashiwara form''' is the [[quadratic form]] on <math>A_1\oplus A_2\oplus\cdots\oplus A_k</math>
<math display="block">\kappa(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k) = \omega(a_1,a_2) + \omega(a_2,a_3)+\cdots+\omega(a_{k-1},a_k) + \omega(a_k,a_1).</math>
The Maslov index is the [[inertial index]] of the form <math>\kappa</math>.<ref name="LionVergne1980" /><ref name="CappellLeeMiller1994">{{cite journal
 |last1=Cappell
 |first1=S. E.
 |last2=Lee
 |first2=Ronnie
 |last3=Miller
 |first3=E. Y.
 |title=On the Maslov index
 |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics
 |volume=47
 |issue=2
 |year=1994
 |pages=121–186
}}</ref> When the subspaces are mutually transverse, the cycle <math>A_1,\dots,A_k,A_1</math> can be realized as a polygon in <math>\Lambda_n</math>, such that <math>A_{k+1}</math> is the graph of a symmetric transformation <math>S:A_k\to A_{k-1}</math>,
<math display="block">A_{k+1} = \{x + Sx \mid x \in A_k\}.</math>
Then the edge <math>A_kA_{k+1}</math> in the polygon is parameterized by <math>u\in[0,1]</math>, <math>\{x + uSx\mid x\in A_k\}</math>.<ref name="LionVergne1980" />

=== For paths of symplectic matrices ===

The Maslov index can also be attached to a path in the [[symplectic group]] <math>\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbf{R})</math>. If <math>\Phi_t</math> is a path of symplectic matrices and <math>L</math> is a fixed Lagrangian subspace, then the path <math>\Phi_t(L)</math> in the Lagrangian Grassmannian has a Maslov index. In this form the invariant is closely related to the [[Conley-Zehnder index]] and to stability questions for periodic orbits of Hamiltonian systems.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

== Basic properties ==

The Maslov index satisfies several formal properties.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

* '''Homotopy invariance''': it is unchanged under homotopies through paths with fixed admissible endpoints.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />
* '''Additivity under concatenation''': if two paths can be concatenated, the Maslov index of the concatenated path is the sum of the indices.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />
* '''Naturality''': symplectic automorphisms preserve the Maslov index.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />
* '''Direct sum property''': for product symplectic spaces, the Maslov index is additive under direct sums of paths.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />
* '''Normalization''': a generator of <math>\pi_1(\Lambda(V))</math> has Maslov index <math>1</math> or <math>2</math>, depending on conventions.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

Different authors adopt slightly different normalizations, especially when comparing the Maslov index of Lagrangian paths, the Maslov class, and the Conley-Zehnder index.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" /><ref name="CappellLeeMiller1994" />

== Low-dimensional example ==

In the standard symplectic plane <math>(\mathbf{R}^2,\omega=dx\wedge dy)</math>, every one-dimensional subspace is Lagrangian, so the Lagrangian Grassmannian can be identified with the real projective line <math>\mathbf{RP}^1</math>. A path of Lagrangian lines is therefore a path of unoriented lines through the origin.<ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" /><ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

Fixing the horizontal axis as reference, the Maslov cycle consists of the single point represented by that axis. The Maslov index of a generic loop counts how many times, with sign and appropriate normalization, the moving line passes through the horizontal direction. In this dimension the Maslov index is closely related to the [[winding number]].<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

== Maslov class ==

There is a universal cohomology class
:<math>\mu \in H^1(\Lambda(V);\mathbf{Z}),</math>
called the '''Maslov class'''. The Maslov index of a loop is obtained by pairing this class with the homology class of the loop.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" />

If <math>L</math> is a [[Lagrangian submanifold]] of a symplectic manifold <math>(M,\omega)</math>, the Gauss map of <math>L</math> takes values in an appropriate Lagrangian Grassmannian bundle. Pulling back the universal Maslov class gives a cohomology class in <math>H^1(L;\mathbf{Z})</math>, also called the Maslov class of the Lagrangian submanifold. Its vanishing is an important condition in symplectic topology and Floer theory.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" />

== Applications ==

=== Geometric optics and caustics ===

In geometric optics, the eikonal equation determines a [[Lagrangian submanifold]]
<math>\Lambda\subset T^*X</math>. Away from caustics, the projection
<math>\pi|_\Lambda:\Lambda\to X</math> is locally a diffeomorphism, so
<math>\Lambda</math> can be written locally as the graph of <math>dS</math>,
and one obtains a WKB solution of the form
<math display="block">u_h(x)\sim a(x)e^{iS(x)/h}.</math>
A caustic occurs when this projection ceases to be regular, so that the single-phase
description breaks down.<ref name="Duistermaat1996" /><ref name="Hormander1971" />

In ray coordinates, the amplitude contains a Jacobian factor
<math display="block">a(x)\propto \left|\det\frac{\partial x}{\partial \alpha}\right|^{-1/2},</math>
which becomes singular at a caustic. Near a generic fold caustic, the local model is
given by the [[Airy function]]. Its oscillatory asymptotics,
<math display="block">\operatorname{Ai}(-z)\sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}\,z^{1/4}}
\sin\!\left(\frac23 z^{3/2}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),</math>
display the phase shift that is encoded globally by the Maslov index.<ref name="Duistermaat1996" /><ref name="DLMF-Airy">{{cite web
 |title=DLMF §9.7(ii): Poincaré-Type Expansions
 |website=NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
 |publisher=National Institute of Standards and Technology
 |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/9.7
 |access-date=2026-03-28
}}</ref>

=== Fourier integral operators ===

The Maslov index also appears in the theory of [[Fourier integral operator]]s.
If an oscillatory integral is written using two different phase functions that
parametrize the same Lagrangian submanifold, the [[method of stationary phase]]
relates the two expressions. The transformation law contains the factor
<math display="block">
|\det \partial^2_{\theta\theta}\Phi|^{-1/2}
e^{\,i\pi\,\operatorname{sgn}(\partial^2_{\theta\theta}\Phi)/4},
</math>
so the signature of the Hessian contributes a phase defined modulo
integer multiples of <math>\pi/2</math>.<ref name="Hormander1971" /><ref name="Duistermaat1996" />

Globally, these local phase ambiguities are encoded by the
Keller–Maslov bundle, and the principal symbol of a Fourier integral operator
is naturally a half-density twisted by that bundle.<ref name="Hormander1971" /><ref name="Duistermaat1996" />

=== Semiclassical analysis ===

The Maslov index appears in [[Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin method|WKB theory]] and related semiclassical approximations as a phase correction. When an oscillatory solution passes through a caustic, the phase jumps by a multiple of <math>\pi/2</math>. This correction is encoded by the Maslov index.<ref name="Duistermaat1996" /><ref name="Hormander1971" />

For this reason the invariant is fundamental in the asymptotic study of wave propagation, [[Fourier integral operator]]s, and [[quantization condition]]s in classical and quantum mechanics.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="Duistermaat1996" />

=== Microlocal analysis ===

In the theory of Fourier integral operators, phase functions may be replaced under changes of coordinates or generating functions. The resulting phase ambiguity is controlled by the Maslov index, which governs the correct choice of half-density and phase factor.<ref name="Hormander1971" /><ref name="Duistermaat1996" />

=== Symplectic topology ===

In [[Floer homology]] and the theory of [[pseudoholomorphic curve]]s, Maslov-type indices determine gradings, expected dimensions of moduli spaces, and transversality formulas. For a Lagrangian submanifold, the Maslov class enters the definition of monotonicity and the construction of Lagrangian Floer homology.<ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" />

=== Hamiltonian dynamics ===

For periodic orbits and linearized Hamiltonian flows, Maslov-type indices measure spectral flow and stability. In this setting they are closely related to the Morse index, the Conley-Zehnder index, and the theory of [[symplectic path]]s.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

== Generalizations ==

Several related invariants are often described as Maslov indices or Maslov-type indices.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" /><ref name="CappellLeeMiller1994" />

* The '''[[Conley–Zehnder index]]''' for paths of symplectic matrices.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />
* The '''Robbin–Salamon index''', which extends the Maslov index to more general symplectic paths.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />
* The Maslov class of a Lagrangian submanifold in a symplectic manifold.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" />

These constructions agree in overlapping settings but are adapted to different geometric and analytic problems.<ref name="CappellLeeMiller1994" />

=== Infinite-dimensional generalizations ===

The Maslov index also has infinite-dimensional analogues, especially for paths in the
Fredholm–Lagrangian Grassmannian of a symplectic Hilbert space. An early formulation
in this direction was given by Nobukazu Otsuki and Kenro Furutani for Lagrangian
intersections in real Hilbert spaces,<ref name="OtsukiFurutani1991">{{cite journal
 |last1=Otsuki
 |first1=Nobukazu
 |last2=Furutani
 |first2=Kenro
 |title=Spectral Flow and Maslov Index Arising from Lagrangian Intersections
 |journal=Tokyo Journal of Mathematics
 |volume=14
 |issue=1
 |year=1991
 |pages=135–150
}}</ref> and a widely cited functional-analytic definition for continuous curves in the
Fredholm–Lagrangian Grassmannian was developed by Bernhelm Booss-Bavnbek and
Kenro Furutani.<ref name="BoossFurutani1998">{{cite journal
 |last1=Booss-Bavnbek
 |first1=Bernhelm
 |last2=Furutani
 |first2=Kenro
 |title=The Maslov Index: a Functional Analytical Definition and the Spectral Flow Formula
 |journal=Tokyo Journal of Mathematics
 |volume=21
 |issue=1
 |year=1998
 |pages=1–34
}}</ref> In this setting the Maslov index is closely related to [[spectral flow]] and
to index theory for families of self-adjoint Fredholm operators.<ref name="CappellLeeMiller1994" /><ref name="BoossFurutani1998" />
A standard review is Furutani's article on the Fredholm–Lagrangian Grassmannian.<ref name="Furutani2004">{{cite journal
 |last=Furutani
 |first=Kenro
 |title=Fredholm–Lagrangian–Grassmannian and the Maslov index
 |journal=Journal of Geometry and Physics
 |volume=51
 |issue=3
 |year=2004
 |pages=269–331
}}</ref>

== History ==

The index is named after the Soviet mathematician and physicist [[Viktor Pavlovich Maslov]], who introduced it in the study of asymptotic solutions of differential equations. It was later given a more explicitly topological interpretation by [[Vladimir Arnold]], who related it to the topology of the Lagrangian Grassmannian and its universal cohomology class.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="LionVergne1980" />

Subsequent work connected the Maslov index with Fourier integral operators, spectral theory, and modern symplectic topology.<ref name="Hormander1971" /><ref name="Duistermaat1996" /><ref name="McDuffSalamon2017" />
